summary:
The Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA ocean-surface-current data into music you can see and hear. Using NASA OSCAR near-real-time currents for the Indian Ocean (10°S to 10°N, 60°E to 90°E) in October 2026, we built a static website that flies from a globe into the region and plays a 4.5-minute piece generated from the data. Current direction sets pitch, speed sets loudness, and longitude sets stereo position, so the music grows as the month's currents strengthen (mean cell speed rose from about 0.16 to 0.24 m/s). A Research Lab lets anyone trace every note to its grid cell, date and value, with CSV and JSON export. Sound is optional and off by default; live captions, keyboard grid navigation and text readouts give blind and low-vision users the same information. The project makes satellite-derived ocean data approachable for the public while staying verifiable for researchers.

Access the site: https://eberjohns.github.io/ocean-notes/
details:
WHAT IT DOES

When you press Play, current particles flow across a relief(height) map while a 4:30 min long piece plays: one day of October 2026 is four bars at 110 BPM, so the month is one composition and the timeline slider is the playhead. Research Lab page shows exact u, v, speed and direction for any cell and date, time series, and exports.

HOW IT WORKS

Offline Python scripts read the 31 daily OSCAR files, crop to the region, and write (1) an 8x8 grid for audio and readouts and (2) a 0.25-degree binary grid for the particles. In the browser, a Web Audio synthesizer maps data to sound: direction to pitch (16 sectors on a scale), latitude to register, mean speed to loudness and note density, longitude to stereo pan. All voices are synthesized; no samples or recordings are used. The same data always produces the same notes.

WHY IT MATTERS

Surface currents carry heat, nutrients and pollution, but a vector map is hard to read for many people. Sound adds a second channel, and the text and keyboard path makes the data usable by blind and low-vision users. Because every note is traceable, the music is an honest view of the data and not a decoration.

TOOLS

Python and NumPy (data preparation), TypeScript, Vite, three.js (rendering), Web Audio API (synthesis), Static hosting - GitHub Pages.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

The month is composed as one piece with a natural crescendo taken from the data. A globe-to-region dive and synchronized particles and music form the signature moment. Data encoding (fixed by the numbers) is kept separate from arrangement (instrument choices), and the interface labels both.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

OSCAR is model-derived from satellite and in situ inputs, not a direct measurement, and the site says so. We use a fixed 0 to 1.0 m/s color and loudness scale so days can be compared. Sound is off by default and no information exists only in sound or only in color.
dataRefs: NASA OSCAR L4 Ocean Surface Currents, Near Real-Time v2.0 (PO.DAAC)
